findings.title: _truncate_output discards serialized string on fast path; _atomic_append re-serializes unconditionally
findings.description: _truncate_output (line 72) calls json.dumps(obj) to measure byte size, then returns obj unmodified when overhead <= 0 (the common path — payload under 1MB). _atomic_append (line 100) immediately calls json.dumps(obj) again on the same dict. Every hook invocation therefore performs two full serializations of the payload; the first is wasted on the common path. For pre-event payloads the waste is unconditional: they never have an output key, so _truncate_output hits the fast-path exit at line 74 or the no-output-key exit at line 77, both discarding serialized. Then _atomic_append re-serializes. For a 300KB Bash post payload (tool_response with large stdout), CPython json.dumps takes roughly 3-8ms, so each such call wastes 3-8ms. At high hook-firing frequency (every tool call), this is a consistent, measurable overhead. The fix is a one-line refactor: thread serialized out of _truncate_output so _atomic_append can use it directly.
findings.fix_sketch: Change _truncate_output to return tuple[dict, str|None]. Fast path returns (obj, serialized). Slow path returns (obj, None) after truncating. Update _atomic_append signature to accept optional pre_serialized: bytes|None. At line 253-255: obj, cached_str = _truncate_output(payload, _max_line_bytes()); _atomic_append(log_file, obj, (cached_str+'\n').encode('utf-8') if cached_str else None). This eliminates the redundant json.dumps on every sub-1MB call.

findings.title: 9 sequential echo|grep subprocess pipelines per Bash call on the no-block path
findings.description: safety-block.sh (added in this PR) fires on every Bash PreToolUse event. Lines 24, 29, 34, 39, 44, 49, 54, 59, and 63 each execute 'echo "$S" | grep -qE ...' — one independent pipeline per destructive pattern. On macOS (system bash 3.2, no lastpipe), each echo|grep pipeline forks 2 processes. Nine patterns × 2 forks = 18 forks per Bash call on the no-block path (normal operation). At 2-5ms per fork+exec on macOS, that is 18-54ms of fork overhead per Bash call added by this single hook. Combined with block-rm-rf.sh (1 jq + 2 sed + 2 grep = 5 forks) and block-push-main.sh (1 jq + 2 sed + 2 grep = 5 forks), the three Bash safety hooks spawn 28 child processes per normal Bash tool call, adding 28-90ms before the python3 logging hook runs. The logging consolidation reduced logging from ~165ms to ~41ms (a ~124ms win); safety-block.sh re-introduces ~18-54ms on every Bash call.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a combined fast-exit guard at the top of the check block: if ! printf '%s' "$S" | grep -qE 'pattern1|pattern2|...|pattern9'; then exit 0; fi. This single 2-fork pipeline handles the no-block path. Only when the combined pattern fires (rare) do the 9 individual if-then-grep blocks execute to produce the correct block message. Net: common-case cost drops from 18 forks to 2 forks (~16-52ms saved per Bash call). Alternatively, consolidate block-rm-rf.sh, block-push-main.sh, and safety-block.sh into a single script, eliminating 2 bash process startups plus their jq/sed/grep children (saves another ~10ms).

residual_risks.description: _pair_key (line 138) calls json.dumps(tool_input, sort_keys=True) on every pre and post invocation to hash the input for the temp-file correlation path. For Write/Edit pre calls with large file content (e.g., 200KB), this serializes the content an extra time beyond the payload serialization in _truncate_output/_atomic_append. The extra cost is ~2ms for 200KB — low in isolation — but it compounds with PERF-001. A lighter pairing key (e.g., hash of session_id + tool_name + file_path only) would avoid serializing the content for the hash while preserving correlation correctness.

call_id is generated by two separate _call_id() calls within the pre event handler: once at line 179 (written to the temp pair-file) and once at line 188 (written to the JSONL log entry). Since _call_id() uses int(time.time()*1_000_000), the two calls produce different values microseconds apart. The pair-file call_id and the log call_id do not match. Pre and post JSONL entries cannot be correlated by call_id — they share only session_id and temporal proximity. Not a performance issue; noted because it affects downstream log queries expecting call_id to join pre/post rows.

_redact_value runs all 8 regex patterns on the full tool_response before _truncate_output reduces it. If Claude Code ever passes >1MB output to hooks (e.g., a large MCP response), 8 regex passes over 1MB = ~8MB of scanning on CPython, estimated 50-200ms. The 1MB JSONL cap is enforced after redaction, not before. The expected behavior of Claude Code's protocol (truncating hook payloads at the source) likely prevents this in practice, but it is not verified in this review.

testing_gaps.description: No automated test measures end-to-end per-call hook latency. The ~41ms target is documented and was measured manually during development, but no regression test would catch a future import addition or synchronous operation that degrades it.

No test covers the _truncate_output fast-path wasted serialization. If PERF-001 is fixed by threading serialized bytes through to _atomic_append, there is no test that would prevent a future refactor from reintroducing the redundant json.dumps.
